/-!
# Conjecture 4.34

by M. I. Kargapolov

Let $v$ be a group word, and let $\mathfrak{K}_v$ be the class of groups $G$ such
that there exists a positive integer $n = n(G)$ such that each element of the
verbal subgroup $vG$ can be represented as a product of $n$ values of the word
$v$ on the group $G$.

a) For which $v$ do all finitely generated soluble groups belong to the class
$\mathfrak{K}_v$?

b) Does the word $v(x, y) = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ satisfy this condition?

Part a) asks for a description of a class of words and is not stated here.
Part b) is stated below.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

blocks.code:
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«4.34».parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Group.FG G] [IsSolvable G],
      ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ ∀ g ∈ commutator G,
        ∃ x y : Fin n → G, (List.ofFn fun i ↦ ⁅x i, y i⁆).prod = g := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
Does the word $v(x, y) = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ satisfy the condition of Problem 4.34, i.e.
does every finitely generated soluble group $G$ belong to the class $\mathfrak{K}_v$?

For this word the verbal subgroup $vG$ is the derived subgroup $[G, G]$, and the set of
values of $v$ on $G$ is the set of commutators of $G$. So the question is: for every
finitely generated soluble group $G$, does there exist a positive integer $n = n(G)$
(depending on $G$) such that every element of $[G, G]$ is a product
$[x_1, y_1] [x_2, y_2] \cdots [x_n, y_n]$ of $n$ commutators of elements of $G$?

The set of values of $x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ on $G$ coincides with the set of Mathlib
commutators `⁅x, y⁆ = x * y * x⁻¹ * y⁻¹`, since $x^{-1} y^{-1} x y = [x^{-1}, y^{-1}]$ in
Mathlib's convention.

claims.decomposer_note: Open-ended characterization of the set of group words v (the deliverable is a description); no candidate answer is asserted in the statement or background, so there is no definite Prop to state — note n = n(G) is allowed to depend on G, and 'soluble' means solvable.

claims.decomposer_note: Yes/no question: for every finitely generated soluble group G, does there exist a positive integer n = n(G) (depending on G, not uniform) such that every element of the derived subgroup [G,G] is a product of n commutators; since 1 = [1,1] and commutator values are closed under inversion, 'exactly n' and 'at most n' factors agree, and the set of values of x^{-1}y^{-1}xy coincides with the set of Mathlib commutators ⁅x,y⁆ = xyx⁻¹y⁻¹.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same faithful proposition (∀ f.g. soluble G, ∃ n > 0 depending on G, every element of commutator G is an ordered product of exactly n commutators); I verified in Lean that commutator G = ⁅⊤,⊤⁆ and that the value set of x⁻¹y⁻¹xy equals commutatorSet G, so using Mathlib's ⁅x,y⁆ is exact. c03 chosen for the repository naming convention (theorem kourovka.«4.34».parts.b inside namespace Kourovka.«4.34», as in the other Kourovka files), the transparent `Fin n → G` + `List.ofFn` ordered product (no reliance on Set.mem_pow as in c07), and a docstring that explains the commutator-convention translation. c01/c04 (literal word) and c02/c05/c06/c08 are equally faithful; c01/c02/c04 deviate from the naming convention (c01 yields Kourovka.«4.34».parts.b via a nested `parts` namespace). No edits were needed; file compiles with only the sorry warning.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 4.34

by M. I. Kargapolov

Let $v$ be a group word, and let $\mathfrak{K}_v$ be the class of groups $G$ such
that there exists a positive integer $n = n(G)$ such that each element of the
verbal subgroup $vG$ can be represented as a product of $n$ values of the word

$\mathfrak{K}_v$?

b) Does the word $v(x, y) = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ satisfy this condition?

Part a) asks for a description of a class of words and is not stated here.
Part b) is stated below.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«4.34»

/--
Does the word $v(x, y) = x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ satisfy the condition of Problem 4.34, i.e.
does every finitely generated soluble group $G$ belong to the class $\mathfrak{K}_v$?

For this word the verbal subgroup $vG$ is the derived subgroup $[G, G]$, and the set of
values of $v$ on $G$ is the set of commutators of $G$. So the question is: for every
finitely generated soluble group $G$, does there exist a positive integer $n = n(G)$
(depending on $G$) such that every element of $[G, G]$ is a product
$[x_1, y_1] [x_2, y_2] \cdots [x_n, y_n]$ of $n$ commutators of elements of $G$?

The set of values of $x^{-1} y^{-1} x y$ on $G$ coincides with the set of Mathlib
commutators `⁅x, y⁆ = x * y * x⁻¹ * y⁻¹`, since $x^{-1} y^{-1} x y = [x^{-1}, y^{-1}]$ in
Mathlib's convention.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«4.34».parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Group.FG G] [IsSolvable G],
      ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ ∀ g ∈ commutator G,
        ∃ x y : Fin n → G, (List.ofFn fun i ↦ ⁅x i, y i⁆).prod = g := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«4.34»

items: The verbal subgroup vG for v = x⁻¹y⁻¹xy is taken to be Mathlib's `commutator G` (the derived subgroup, generated by all ⁅x,y⁆); the values of v are taken to be Mathlib commutators ⁅x, y⁆ = x*y*x⁻¹*y⁻¹. The value sets coincide since x⁻¹y⁻¹xy = ⁅x⁻¹, y⁻¹⁆ (checked in a scratch proof: {x⁻¹*y⁻¹*x*y} = commutatorSet G).

"Product of n values" is formalized as a product of exactly n commutators via `(List.ofFn fun i ↦ ⁅x i, y i⁆).prod` for x y : Fin n → G, with `0 < n` kept literally from the source (positive integer). Since 1 = ⁅1,1⁆, 'exactly n' and 'at most n' agree, and the 0 < n restriction changes nothing mathematically.
Groups are quantified over `Type` (universe 0), following the other Kourovka files (1_40, 19_25, 1_74, 20_76); finitely generated groups are countable so this loses no generality.
Finitely generated is `Group.FG G` and soluble is `IsSolvable G` (derived series terminates), used as instance-implicit binders inside the ∀.
Part a) ('For which v …') is dropped per the decomposition table and only described in the module docstring.

reviewer_notes: Part a) ('For which v ...') was correctly dropped by the decomposition table: it asks for a description of a class of words and has no statable Prop; all candidates agreed. Modeling notes for part b): 'exactly n' vs 'at most n' agree because 1 = ⁅1,1⁆; the positivity requirement 0 < n is kept verbatim and is mathematically immaterial; groups are quantified over `Type` (universe 0), which loses no generality for finitely generated groups and follows the other Kourovka files. Mathlib's commutator convention ⁅x,y⁆ = xyx⁻¹y⁻¹ differs from the notebook's x⁻¹y⁻¹xy, but the value sets coincide (x⁻¹y⁻¹xy = ⁅x⁻¹,y⁻¹⁆), checked with a scratch Lean proof.
